This document is the working task list for the RestoreDART results, converted from
the plain-text `TODO` file. It has two parts: the caveats that apply to every figure
and table in `2_make_DART_results.Rmd`, and the outstanding analysis and reporting
tasks, grouped by theme rather than by the order in which they were written down.

**Review status.** Every task below has been checked against `2_make_DART_results.Rmd`
as it currently stands (716 lines). Items that the current results address adequately
are ~~struck through~~ and followed by an italic *Addressed:* note giving the line
range and the chunk label where the work lives. Items that are only partially covered
carry a *Partly addressed:* note saying what exists and what is still missing, and
items with no coverage carry an *Outstanding:* note. A few items resolved by a
decision to **not** do the work are struck as well, with the note recording where
that decision is documented. Line numbers refer to `2_make_DART_results.Rmd` and will
drift as that file is edited.

Of the 20 task entries, 12 are struck in full, along with the last of the four
collaborator sub-questions; 3 are partly addressed, 4 are outstanding, and 1 (the
de-prioritisation of publication graphics) is a standing priority note rather than a
task. The four fully outstanding items are the model `.Rmd` split, time metrics in the
summary table, a stability-over-time metric, and a late-year sample-size cut-off.

## Caveats and considerations

These apply to all of the figures and tables in the current results document and
should be restated wherever those results are presented.

- **Objectives are not mutually exclusive.** The objective groupings count a pixel as
  part of an objective if that pixel fell within *any* part of the defined objective.
  Multi-objective treatments are therefore included in several objective groupings at
  once, and substantial parts of the dataset are counted more than once across the
  figures and tables. Counts and percentages should be read as per-objective summaries,
  not as a partition of the dataset. *This caveat is now quantified rather than just
  stated: the co-occurrence table in chunk `results-1_22` (lines 555-602) reports how
  many of the current objective's pixels carried no second objective, and how many
  carried each of the others.*
- **Objective/response pairings are restricted.** An objective/response combination is
  only included if the response variable is the same cover type as the objective's
  target cover (for example, `decrease_afg` paired with the differenced AFG response).
  The single exception is bare ground, which is shown in combination with every
  objective because it is informative regardless of which cover type was targeted.

## Time effects

This is the largest open block of work. The overall aim is to describe *when* after
treatment an effect appears, how long it persists, and how confident we can be in
that timing given the available sample.

- ~~**Separate out significance by time in the same way it is already separated by
  ecoregion and treatment.** At minimum this is needed for visualisation, so that the
  time dimension can be read off a figure the same way the ecoregion and treatment
  dimensions can.~~
  *Addressed: chunk `results-1_17`, lines 352-400. `sig_by_year` tabulates percent
  significant, percent significant positive and percent significant negative for each
  year since treatment, and `plot_sig_direction_stacked()` draws the same three
  quantities as a stacked bar per year with sample-size labels. The by-treatment and
  by-ecoregion versions of the timing summary follow in chunk `results-1_20`
  (lines 507-533).*
- ~~**Decide whether to bin time.** Binning would stabilise the per-year estimates at
  the cost of temporal resolution; 5-, 10- and 15+-year bins are the obvious starting
  point. This needs a decision rather than being left implicit.~~
  *Addressed - decided in favour of binning, in addition to the per-year table: chunk
  `results-1_19`, lines 452-480. `cut()` at line 454 defines the 1-5, 6-10, 11-15 and
  16+ bins and `sig_by_bin` reports total pixels and mean percent significant (overall
  and by direction) within each bin, tagged with objective and cover so it can be bound
  across objectives.*
- ~~**Identify the year at which treatment was most and least effective**, where
  effectiveness is quantified as the percentage of significant DART pixels.~~
  *Addressed: chunk `results-1_17`, lines 380-386, with the result written out as prose
  at lines 398-399. Both the year and its percent significant are pulled from
  `sig_by_year` with inline R rather than typed in, so they cannot drift from the table
  immediately above them.*
- ~~**Summarise per-polygon timing, then aggregate across polygons.** Compute the mean,
  minimum, maximum and standard deviation of the percentage of significant pixels,
  along with the 5/10/15+-year bins, and answer the question "how far in time was the
  treatment most significant?". Doing this within each polygon first should mitigate
  the sample size problems that arise when years are pooled across polygons.~~
  *Addressed: chunk `results-1_20`, lines 482-533. `poly_year_sig` computes percent
  significant per polygon × year, `poly_best_worst` reduces each polygon to its
  highest- and lowest-significance year, and `time_summary_by_tx` /
  `time_summary_by_eco` aggregate those per-polygon peak years across polygons with N,
  mean, SD, min and max, reported separately by treatment and by ecoregion. The header
  comment at lines 483-488 records that this is a hard per-polygon peak, unweighted and
  unsmoothed. SD is blanked rather than printed as `NA` for single-polygon groups
  (lines 534-543). The year bins requested in the same item are in chunk `results-1_19`.*
  - ~~**Caveat: censoring.** A polygon whose maximum or minimum effect falls at the end
    of its available time series is censored, and its true peak may lie beyond the
    observation window. This needs to be flagged, and ideally quantified as the number
    of polygons whose extremum occurs in the final year.~~
    *Addressed: chunk `results-1_20`, lines 502-503 flag `is_censored_max` and
    `is_censored_min` per polygon, and lines 516 and 528 report `pct_censored_max` -
    the percentage of polygons whose peak lands on their last observed year - in both
    the by-treatment and by-ecoregion tables. The same flag is carried for the
    mean-effect peak in chunk `results-1_18b` (`peak_effect_year()`, lines 405-430) and
    surfaced in the peak-effect prose bullets. The interpretation is written out at
    line 545.*
- ~~**Define what a "non-significant" time effect is.** One option is to inverse-weight
  the time-series summary statistics by the overall magnitude of significance within
  that time series, so that polygons with weak or noisy signals contribute less to the
  aggregate timing estimate. If that is done, decide whether the variance metrics
  (standard deviation, standard error) can and should be weighted the same way.~~
  *Addressed - resolved by deciding against weighting. Line 350 states that no
  weighting is used anywhere in the time section, that weighting schemes were tested,
  and that they did not improve the results, with the analysis itself in
  `weight_testing_summary.Rmd`. Lines 547-549 record the removal of the
  significance-weighted peak-year summaries and their helper functions
  (`weighted_peak_year()`, `plot_weighted_peak_heatmap()`), on the grounds that a
  fractional "centre of mass" year is not interpretable in the response's own units and
  silently blends the two effect directions. The unweighted mean-effect-by-year table
  and figure in chunk `results-1_18b` (lines 405-450) answer the underlying question
  instead.*
  - ~~Mean time to maximum treatment effect, weighted by the magnitude of the effect,
    per polygon on the y axis, against treatment or ecoregion on the x axis.~~
  - ~~A heatmap with treatment and ecoregion on the x and y axes and mean time to
    maximum significance as the fill.~~
    *Both superseded by the same decision: these were the weighted figures removed at
    lines 547-549. Their unweighted replacements are the per-treatment and
    per-ecoregion peak-year tables in chunk `results-1_20` (lines 507-533).*
- ~~**Quantify how much polygon-level variability the weighting scheme discards.** We
  need results that describe how poorly the polygons capture variability in effects
  through time - concretely, how many polygons are effectively ignored once a
  weighting scheme is applied.~~
  *Addressed - and partly moot, since no weighting scheme survives (line 350), so no
  polygons are being down-weighted out of the summaries. The underlying question of how
  variable the timing is between polygons is answered directly and unweighted in chunk
  `results-1_20`: the SD, min and max of the per-polygon peak year (lines 507-533) show
  the spread across polygons within each treatment and ecoregion, and `pct_censored_max`
  says what share of polygons cannot be placed at all because their peak is censored.*
- **Quantify stability over time.** Whether an effect, once significant, stays
  significant is a separate question from when it first appears, and needs its own
  metric.
  *Outstanding: no persistence or stability metric is computed. The per-polygon work in
  chunk `results-1_20` (lines 482-506) identifies each polygon's single best and worst
  year but says nothing about runs of consecutive significant years, and line 545 flags
  the stable-state-change discussion as a consequence of censoring without measuring it.
  `poly_year_sig` (lines 489-497) is already at the polygon × year grain a run-length or
  autocorrelation metric would need.*
- ~~**Add uncertainty around the significant-pixel percentages.** The standard error or
  standard deviation around the count of statistically significant pixels can be
  reported for overall significance by computing it across polygons, treating each
  polygon as the unit of replication.~~
  *Addressed: chunk `results-1_12b`, lines 203-226. `summarize_poly_sig()` collapses to
  one percent-significant value per polygon and then reports the mean, SD and SE of
  that per-polygon rate, separately for the overall, significant-positive and
  significant-negative rates. The rationale - that pixels within a polygon are
  spatially correlated and so are not independent observations - is stated at line 201,
  and the same three metrics are drawn with ± 1 SE ranges in chunk `results-1_12c`
  (lines 228-236).*

  *Addressed: the spatial versions exist in three places. Chunk `results-1_15`

## Sample size and polygon standardisation

- **Standardise polygons on the basis of their time series.** Check that a small number
  of polygons with unusually long records are not extending the overall time series and
  dominating the visualisations.
  *Partly addressed: the diagnostic exists but no standardisation is applied. Chunk
  `results-1_11b` (lines 183-185) plots, for each year since treatment, how many
  distinct polygons contribute at least one pixel, which is where a thinning tail would
  show up; `poly_best_worst` also records `n_years` per polygon (line 499). What is
  missing is any action taken on that diagnostic - no polygon is trimmed or reweighted
  on the basis of record length, and the per-year figures still run to the full extent
  of the longest-record polygons.*
- **Consider a sample size cut-off for polygons after a given year**, so that years
  supported by only a handful of polygons are not plotted or summarised as though they
  were as well supported as the early years.
  *Outstanding: the only sample-size cut-off in the document is the `min_txeco_n <- 300`
  pixel threshold on treatment × ecoregion combinations (line 47, applied in chunks
  `results-1_4` and `results-1_6`), which is cross-sectional and does nothing about
  sparsely supported late years. A year-based or polygon-count-based threshold would
  attach to `sig_by_year` (lines 352-366) and to the per-year figures.*
- ~~**Add time sample size tables to the `.Rmd`.** Specifically, are sample sizes in the
  later years being reduced, and is that reduction affecting the results
  disproportionately? These tables are the evidence base for the cut-off decision
  above.~~
  *Addressed: three complementary views. Chunk `results-1_11b` (lines 183-185) gives
  polygons contributing per year since treatment; chunk `results-1_17` carries a
  `n_pix` total-pixel column per year in `sig_by_year` (lines 352-366) and labels every
  bar in the stacked figure with both its group total and its per-direction significant
  counts (lines 369-373, explained at lines 388-396); and chunk `results-1_19`
  (lines 456-480) reports total pixels per year bin. Whether the late-year reduction is
  distorting the results is the judgement the cut-off item above still has to make, but
  the numbers needed to make it are now in the document.*

management goal.

- When decreasing tree cover was the goal, what do the AFG, SHR and PFG group
  directions look like?
- When increasing PFG cover was the goal, what do the AFG directions look like?
- When decreasing shrub cover was the goal, what do the AFG, PFG and TRE directions
  look like?
  *Partly addressed - written but not running. All three questions are coded in chunk
  `results_total` (lines 604-620) as `compare_related_directions()` calls on
  `combined_df` (lines 607, 612 and 617), each returning a table of percent significant

  Turning it on is the remaining step; note that these calls start from `combined_df`
  rather than the filtered `s_0$input`, so their denominators are the full dataset.*
- ~~How did significant effects change through time, presented in a way we can actually
  talk about (for example, using the time bins discussed above)?~~
  *Addressed: the talkable versions are the prose sentences rather than the raw tables.
  Chunk `results-1_17` emits the most- and least-effective year as sentences at
  lines 398-399; chunk `results-1_18b` builds one bullet per effect direction giving the
  peak year, its mean effect, SE and significant-pixel count, flagging the peak as
  censored where relevant (lines 436-448); and chunk `results-1_19` (lines 452-480)
  provides the 1-5 / 6-10 / 11-15 / 16+ bin table for the coarser statements. Line 450

  the most significant pixels, which is the distinction to keep straight when
  describing these results.*
